photos.title: File:Kimlau Memorial Arch and Statue of Lin Zexu, Chatham Square, Chinatown, Manhattan, New York (7237354944).jpg
photos.artist: Ken Lund from Reno, Nevada, USA
photos.credit: Kimlau Memorial Arch and Statue of Lin Zexu, Chatham Square, Chinatown, Manhattan, New York
photos.description: Chatham Square is a major intersection in Manhattan's Chinatown. The square lies at the confluence of seven streets: Bowery, East Broadway, St. James Place, Mott Street, Oliver Street, Worth Street and Park Row.The Kimlau Memorial Arch was erected by the American Legion, Lt. B.R. Kimlau Post 1291 in 1962 to honor United States service members of Chinese ancestry who have fought and died serving their country. The arch is named after 26-year-old 2nd Lt. Benjamin Ralph Kimlau, an aircraft commander in the 380th Bombardment Group who was shot down on a mission over Los Negros Island on March 5, 1944 during World War II. This memorial, bears calligraphy by famous Chinese calligrapher and poet Yu Youren. There is also a statue of Lin Zexu in the square. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatham_Square,_Manhattan en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Text_of_Creative_Commons_...

photos.title: File:Doyers Street, Chinatown, Manhattan, New York (7237356826).jpg
photos.artist: Ken Lund from Reno, Nevada, USA
photos.credit: Doyers Street, Chinatown, Manhattan, New York
photos.description:
Doyers Street is a street in the heart of Chinatown in the New York City borough of Manhattan. It is one block in length and has a sharp bend in the middle. The street, which is about 200 feet long, runs south and then southeast from Pell Street to Chatham Square. The street is the site of several restaurants and the Chinatown branch of the United States Postal Service at 6 Doyers St.
The Nom Wah Tea Parlor opened at 13 Doyers Street in 1927, and is still in operation. Other longstanding business include Ting's Gift Shop at 18 Doyers. The street is also known for its barber shops and hair stylists.
Early in the century, the bend in the street became known as "the Bloody Angle" because of numerous shootings among the Tong Gangs of Chinatown that lasted into the 1930s. Hatchets were frequently used, leading to the creation of the expression, "hatchet man". In 1994, law enforcement officials said that more people died violently at the "Bloody Angle" than at any other street intersection in the United States.

photos.title: File:The Bowery, Chatham Square, Chinatown, Manhattan, New York (7237355910).jpg
photos.artist: Ken Lund from Reno, Nevada, USA
photos.credit: The Bowery, Chatham Square, Chinatown, Manhattan, New York
photos.description: Bowery, commonly called "the Bowery," is a street and a small neighborhood in the southern portion of the New York City borough of Manhattan. The neighborhood's boundaries are East 4th Street and the East Village to the north, Canal Street and Chinatown to the South, Allen Street and the Lower East Side to the east and Little Italy to the west. Bowery is an anglicisation of the Dutch bouwerij, derived from an antiquated Dutch word for "farm." In the 17th century the road branched off Broadway north of Fort Amsterdam at the tip of Manhattan to the homestead of Peter Stuyvesant, Director-General of New Netherland. As a street, the Bowery was known as Bowery Lane prior to 1807.Today it runs from Chatham Square in the south to Cooper Square at 4th Street in the north. After Cooper Square, the street runs north as Third Avenue and to the northwest as Fourth Avenue. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowery_(Manhattan) en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Text_of_Creative_Commons_...

photos.title: File:Kimlau Memorial Arch.jpg
photos.description: The Kimlau War Memorial in Kimlau Square (Chatham Square) in the Chinatown neighborhood of Manhattan, New York City, was designed by Poy G. Lee in granite and structural steel, with cement used for the finish.  It was was erected in 1961 by the American Legion, Lt. B.R. Kimlau Post 1291 to honor United States service members of Chinese ancestry who fought and died serving the United States, and is named after Benjamin Kimlau, an aircraft commander in the 380th Bombardment Group, who died in World War II. (Source: "NYC Parks Dept: Kimlau Square")

photos.title: File:300 East 4th Street entrance.jpg
photos.description: 300 East 4th Street at the corner of Avenue C in the Loisaida or Alphabet City section of the East Village neighborhood in Manhattan, New York City was built prior to 1915 as Holy Cross House, a Catholic boardinghouse for working girls.  It was designed in the Gothic revival style.  It is currently in use as residences. (Sources: Google book search results and "4th Street" on New York Songlines])

photos.title: File:The first published image of a photograph.jpg
photos.description:
Apparently the first published image of a photograph.
Engraving or woodcut after a photogenic drawing by Dr. Golding Bird. Published in the April 20, 1839 issue of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, illustrating an article "A Treatise on Photogenic Drawing".

photos.title: File:NYCT 94443 (8387200822).jpg
photos.artist: Metropolitan Transportation Authority of the State of New York
photos.description:
Although most subway lines are back to normal after Hurricane Sandy, there is a different story behind the scenes. Workers at New York City Transit's Coney Island Yard are throwing switches by hand as a result of damage from the superstorm.
The yard was pummeled with about four feet of salt water, mounds of storm-driven sand, and sustained high winds.

Photo: Metropolitan Transportation Authority / Patrick Cashin.

photos.artist: Metropolitan Transportation Authority of the State of New York
photos.description:
Although most subway lines are back to normal after Hurricane Sandy, there is a different story behind the scenes. Workers at New York City Transit's Coney Island Yard are throwing switches by hand as a result of damage from the superstorm.
The yard was pummeled with about four feet of salt water, mounds of storm-driven sand, and sustained high winds.
This photo shows Signal Maintainer Victor Cubero operating a switch manually.

Photo: Metropolitan Transportation Authority / Patrick Cashin.

photos.title: File:Beach 116th St Newport Av Bch Channel Dr td (2023-09-04) 35b.jpg
photos.description: A Rockaway Park–Beach 116th Street-bound Q22 local bus pulling up to its terminal stop at the southwest corner of Beach 116th Street and Newport Avenue south of Beach Channel Drive in Rockaway Park, Queens.  Since September 2018, most Q22s end service here instead of traveling farther west to Roxbury and Fort Tilden. Note the destination sign reads "via Ferry", as the terminal loop travels via the Rockaway NYC Ferry terminal on the north shore (Rockaway Inlet). Whether this was deliberate or coincidence is a good question.

photos.title: File:Beach 116th St Newport Av Bch Channel Dr td (2025-08-24) 01b.jpg
photos.description: The current southern/eastern terminal for Q35 buses, at the southwest corner of Newport Avenue and Beach 116th Street south of Beach Channel Drive in Rockaway Park, Queens. Pictured is a new modern European-style sign for the Q22 route. Under the upcoming Queens Bus Redesign, the Q35 will be rerouted south onto Rockaway Beach Boulevard and no longer use this stop. The Q22 will instead use this stop as its new last stop and layover area, but still begin eastbound service at its current first stop on Beach 116th Street.

photos.title: File:Beach 116th St Newport Av Bch Channel Dr td (2025-08-24) 02a.jpg
photos.description: A Rockaway Park–Beach 116th Street-bound Q22 local bus pulling up to its terminal stop, turning south from Beach Channel Drive onto Beach 116th Street at Newport Avenue in Rockaway Park, Queens. Note the destination sign now reads "Rockaway Park–Beach 116 St" instead of the short run programming reading "B. 116 St". Under the upcoming Queens Bus Redesign, the Q22 route will have its now-part-time western leg to Roxbury, Riis Park, and Fort Tilden eliminated, but will be extended on its eastern end to the Far Rockaway LIRR station and the NYCHA Redfern Houses at Nameoke Street, with two trips along the former Q22A route through Bayswater. And still no overnight service.

photos.title: File:Rubus phoenicolasius - Wineberry.jpg
photos.description:
NATIVE RANGE
Japan, Korea and China
DESCRIPTION
Wineberry, or wine raspberry, is a typical species in the genus Rubus, which contains blackberry and raspberry. The name Rubus phoenicolasius translates as "blackberry with purple hairs." The mature plant has long stems (canes) that are upright and arching and covered with distinctive glandular red hairs and small spines. The hairs give the canes a reddish color when seen from a distance. Under favorable conditions, canes may grow to a length of 9 feet. Leaves consist of three heart-shaped, serrated leaflets with purplish veins and are silvery white tomentose on the underside. Small greenish flowers with white petals and reddish hairs occur in Spring. The very edible raspberry like fruit is bright red and ripens during June and July.
BACKGROUND
Wineberry was introduced into the United States in 1890 as breeding stock for new Rubus cultivars. It is used today by berry breeders to add specific genes to berry varieties or species. Wineberry is an example of one man's flower being another man's weed. Given containment, wineberry has desirable and useful qualities, but due to its invasive nature, it is considered a significant pest of agricultural and natural ecosystems. Wineberry has been used as a virus indicator for raspberry yellow spot and wineberry latent virus and numerous plant viruses have been isolated from it.
Source: Plant Conservation Alliance, Alien Plant Working Group.

www.nps.gov/plants/alien/fact/ruph1.htm

photos.title: File:Arthur Kill Station Groundbreaking (10350551926).jpg
photos.artist: Metropolitan Transportation Authority of the State of New York
photos.credit:
Arthur Kill Station Groundbreaking

Uploaded by tm
photos.description:
Scene at groundbreaking ceremony on the site of future Arthur Kill Station. The station, which is scheduled to be completed in 2015, will replace two others, Nassau and Atlantic (pictured), which are deteriorating and can only accommodate one train car. A unique feature of the station will be a 150-car parking lot, to be built across the street, the first such lot on the system.

Photo: Marc A. Hermann / MTA New York City Transit

photos.title: File:Arthur Kill SIR td (2025-08-02) 004b.jpg
photos.description: Looking across at a NYC Subway-style station sign on the St. George-bound platform of the Arthur Kill station on the Main Branch of the Staten Island Railway (SIR / SIRT), along Arthur Kill Road / Ellis Street between Lion Street and Barnard Avenue (at approximately Nashville Street) in Tottenville, Staten Island. The newest station on the line replacing the Atlantic and Nassau factory stations, most of the station shares a similar colorful-but-bare-bones design with the existing SIR stations. Interesting, as new New York City Subway stations are almost always different from previous stations, built in the prevailing architectural style of their time.

photos.title: File:Arthur Kill SIR td (2025-08-02) 006 - Emergency Exit.jpg
photos.description: The emergency exit at the east end of the Tottenville-bound platform of the Arthur Kill station on the Main Branch of the Staten Island Railway (SIR / SIRT), along Arthur Kill Road / Ellis Street between Lion Street and Barnard Avenue (at approximately Nashville Street) in Tottenville, Staten Island. The emergency doors on both platforms have been propped open, with passengers exiting here. Also, with the comedically-low height of both the door and station fencing (similar to the WTC–Cortlandt station), and the fact that no fares are collected here anyway, this all seems quite pointless.

photos.title: File:Arthur Kill SIR td (2025-08-02) 012.jpg
photos.description: A NYC Subway-style station sign at the east end of the Tottenville-bound platform of the Arthur Kill station on the Main Branch of the Staten Island Railway (SIR / SIRT), along Arthur Kill Road / Ellis Street between Lion Street and Barnard Avenue (at approximately Nashville Street) in Tottenville, Staten Island. The newest station on the line replacing the Atlantic and Nassau factory stations, most of the station shares a similar colorful-but-bare-bones design with the existing SIR stations. Interesting, as new New York City Subway stations are almost always different from previous stations, built in the prevailing architectural style of their time.

photos.title: File:Arthur Kill SIR td (2025-08-02) 014 - Emergency Exit.jpg
photos.description: Looking across at the emergency exit at the east end of the St. George-bound platform of the Arthur Kill station on the Main Branch of the Staten Island Railway (SIR / SIRT), along Arthur Kill Road / Ellis Street between Lion Street and Barnard Avenue (at approximately Nashville Street) in Tottenville, Staten Island. The emergency doors on both platforms have been propped open, with passengers exiting here. Also, with the comedically-low height of both the door and station fencing (similar to the WTC–Cortlandt station), and the fact that no fares are collected here anyway, this all seems quite pointless.

photos.title: File:Arthur Kill SIR td (2025-08-02) 017 - CubeSmart.jpg
photos.description: Looking north at a CubeSmart self-storage facility from the Tottenville-bound platform of the Arthur Kill station on the Main Branch of the Staten Island Railway (SIR / SIRT), along Arthur Kill Road / Ellis Street between Lion Street and Barnard Avenue (at approximately Nashville Street) in Tottenville, Staten Island. Although the Atlantic Terra Cotta and Nassau Smelting (Bell Telephone) factories once served by this line have long closed, the northern edge of this area still retains its historical industrial characteristics.

photos.title: File:Arthur Kill SIR td (2025-08-02) 031c.jpg
photos.description:
A Baltimore & Ohio Railroad-style signal at the far west end of the Tottenville-bound platform of the Arthur Kill station on the Main Branch of the Staten Island Railway (SIR / SIRT), along Arthur Kill Road / Ellis Street between Lion Street and Barnard Avenue (at approximately Nashville Street) in Tottenville, Staten Island. One of the signs that the line is still technically part of the national rail network. Or it was just cheaper to maintain the old interlocking system.
Also note the blue sign to the right for checking station elevator status, when this station has ramps instead of elevators.

photos.title: File:Arthur Kill SIR td (2025-08-02) 033 - Entrance and Overpass.jpg
photos.description: The stairs up to the overpass and down to Ellis Street from the Tottenville-bound platform at the west end of the Arthur Kill station on the Main Branch of the Staten Island Railway (SIR / SIRT), along Arthur Kill Road / Ellis Street between Lion Street and Barnard Avenue (at approximately Nashville Street) in Tottenville, Staten Island. This large structure distinguishes this station from the older SIR stations, resembling other suburban intermodal stations. This particular staircase structure reminds me of the entrance to the East 105th Street Canarsie Line station.

photos.title: File:Arthur Kill SIR td (2025-08-02) 036b - Entrance and Overpass.jpg
photos.description: Looking down from the entrance and overpass structure at the plaza on the north side (Ellis Street) of the Arthur Kill station on the Main Branch of the Staten Island Railway (SIR / SIRT), along Arthur Kill Road / Ellis Street between Lion Street and Barnard Avenue (at approximately Nashville Street) in Tottenville, Staten Island. Interesting this landscaped plaza was built on the industrial north side of the station, instead of the residential south side.

photos.title: File:Arthur Kill SIR td (2025-08-02) 042 - Entrance and Overpass.jpg
photos.description: Walking down from the overpass to the St. George-bound platform and Arthur Kill Road entrance at the west end of the Arthur Kill station on the Main Branch of the Staten Island Railway (SIR / SIRT), along Arthur Kill Road / Ellis Street between Lion Street and Barnard Avenue (at approximately Nashville Street) in Tottenville, Staten Island. This large structure distinguishes this station from the older SIR stations, resembling other suburban intermodal stations. Although this structure is large and tall, it consists simply of a metal truss frame and glass panels, missing the "meat" of for example the Howard Beach – JFK Airport station overpass.

photos.title: File:Arthur Kill SIR td (2025-08-02) 039.jpg
photos.description: Looking from the overpass on the Tottenville-bound side at the far west end of the Arthur Kill station on the Main Branch of the Staten Island Railway (SIR / SIRT), along Arthur Kill Road / Ellis Street between Lion Street and Barnard Avenue (at approximately Nashville Street) in Tottenville, Staten Island. Note that the wheelchair ramps on the opposite (St. George-bound) side are on the west end of the platform, extending that platform an additional train car length or so.
